concurrency_primitives: Both datasets loaded in parallel goroutines + WaitGroup (cmd/analyzer/main.go:40-50); per file: scanner goroutine -> bounded jobs chan gated by a credits chan (workers*8) -> N json.Unmarshal parser goroutines -> sequence-restoring dispatcher -> FNV-hashed shard channels (cap 32) each owned by one aggregation goroutine with a private map, merged at end (internal/ingest/ingest.go:40-158); join worker pool over immutable maps with sorted output (internal/analysis/analysis.go:21-65); runtime.GOMAXPROCS(workers); concurrent downloads in cmd/fetch
design_patterns: Pipeline (bounded channel stages: read -> parse -> ordered validate/dedup -> sharded aggregate -> parallel join -> analyses -> report) across cmd/fetch, cmd/analyzer, internal/model, internal/ingest, internal/analysis, internal/report
questions: Which neighborhoods have high counts on both vacancy properties and 311 requests (>=75th midrank percentile on both)?
How does the mix of request types differ between low- and high-vacancy-count neighborhoods?
How do median closure times for the same request types differ between those cohorts?
How do monthly requests change across the selected quarter in each cohort?
Which five neighborhoods rank highest under a transparent 50/50 percentile score, and what is their leading request category?
stakeholders: Joint housing and city-services review team (generic; DHCD / DPW / 311 agencies implied)
overview: A compact, idiomatic Go pipeline in five packages that streams two bundled raw ArcGIS JSONL extracts through credit-bounded parsing pools, an order-restoring dispatcher that validates and deduplicates, FNV-sharded owned-map aggregation, and a parallel neighborhood join, then writes a Markdown report and CSV. Everything is deterministic across worker counts (verified byte-for-byte by verify.sh), covered by 16 tests including a 10k-record stress fixture and a mocked downloader, and documented honestly, with explicit data-quality limits. The only structural weakness is a long report.Write that mixes some analysis thresholds with formatting.
stakeholder_value: The results are real and partly actionable: a credible priority list (Broadway East, Carrollton Ridge, Sandtown-Winchester, Central Park Heights, Harlem Park) and a specific lead that parking complaints take 22 days to close in high-vacancy neighborhoods versus 10 days in low-vacancy ones. Value is limited by the generic stakeholder, three questions that are 311 measures stratified by vacancy cohort rather than two-sided joins, a shallow Q4, and minimal visualization (one ASCII bar block, otherwise tables).
issues: Visualization is minimal: Markdown tables and one ASCII bar chart; no HTML or web UI
Stakeholder is a generic 'joint housing and city-services review team'; no office named per question
Q2-Q4 are single-dataset 311 measures stratified by a vacancy-derived cohort; Q4 (both cohorts -14% Oct->Dec) is shallow
report.Write is a single 155-line function that mixes analysis thresholds with formatting
README and VERIFICATION.md contain leftover assistant-style notes addressed to 'the user' (e.g. 'No Canvas submission has been performed', 'review any course rules concerning outside assistance')
30.8% of raw 311 rows lack a neighborhood and are excluded (documented; inherent to the source)
rationale: Every hard requirement is met and verified: approved language, two real bundled Open Baltimore datasets with matching SHA-256 checksums and provenance manifest, race-free and deterministic goroutine/channel concurrency in parse, aggregate and join stages, bounded memory, a clean tested multi-package pipeline, and a README whose macOS instructions work as written. Deductions are for sparse visualization and a generic stakeholder with stratified rather than two-sided questions, minor mixing of analysis into the report layer, and AI-assistant residue in the docs. 93/100, A.
